Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R34 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: x and y are positive integers, and neither of them is one. Given: x times y is equal to a hundred, and A is equal to the absolute value of x minus y. What is the difference between the greatest possible value of A and the smallest possible value of A?

A long story, but underneath, it's just breaking a hundred into two factors. A is the distance between x and y. The bars make it positive, so it's the bigger one minus the smaller one. And they want the biggest A minus the smallest A. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, listing every pair, and then thinking about the extremes.
at: breaking a hundred into two factors

slides.say: [short pause] Our first method, every pair. I start with the smallest factor and go up. One isn't allowed, so no one times a hundred. Two times fifty, and the difference is forty-eight. Three? A hundred doesn't divide by three. Four times twenty-five, and the difference is twenty-one.
Five times twenty, and the difference is fifteen. Six, seven, eight and nine, none of them divide a hundred. And ten times ten, the difference is zero.

Can I stop here? Yes. Why? After ten, the pairs just come back reversed. Twenty times five is the same pair as five times twenty. Ten is where they meet, because ten times ten is a hundred, ten is the square root.
So the biggest A is forty-eight, and the smallest is zero. Forty-eight minus zero is forty-eight, so choice number three is our answer.
at: choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Now careful, ten times ten is the pair a lot of students forget, because x and y feel like they should be different. Without it, the smallest A is fifteen, and forty-eight minus fifteen is thirty-three. That's choice number one, the trap. And twenty-one and fifteen are just single values of A.
at: ten times ten is the pair

slides.say: [pause] Our second method, the extremes. When is A biggest? When x and y are as far apart as possible, so one of them is as small as it can be. One isn't allowed, so the smallest is two, and the other is a hundred over two, fifty. Fifty minus two is forty-eight.
When is A smallest? When they're as close as possible. Can they be equal? Only if a hundred is a perfect square, and it is, ten times ten. So the smallest A is ten minus ten, zero.
Forty-eight minus zero, forty-eight. Choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
